strengths: The fully-seen/partially-seen training paradigm provides a clear, controlled setting for studying generalization to unseen orientations. Keeping the training image budget fixed helps separate effects of orientation coverage from simply adding data.

The per-orientation heatmaps reveal useful structure hidden by average accuracy: generalization concentrates near observed views and around in-plane and certain silhouette-related transformations. These findings have an identifiable audience in robustness and representation learning.

The experiments cover three object categories, three architectures, different training orientation ranges, cross-category transfer, pretraining, and augmentation. Five repetitions with resampled instance assignments strengthen the empirical observations.

The geometric model and component ablations provide an interpretable descriptive account of the accuracy patterns. The main experimental setup is communicated clearly, and a public data/code repository is identified.
weaknesses: Necessary—support or narrow the central mechanistic claims. The abstract and Discussion assert that shared feature neurons disseminate invariance and that biological recognition mechanisms largely apply to these networks. Figure 4 provides activation examples and correlations, which remain compatible with common view dependence or shared architectural biases. Controlled interventions are needed to identify the proposed mechanism; alternatively, consistently present dissemination as a hypothesis supported by observational associations and the biological connection as an analogy. This claim–evidence gap drives the leaning-reject recommendation.

Necessary—clarify model validation and partition construction. Section 4.2 directly optimizes the Pearson correlation subsequently used to demonstrate predictive power, without describing held-out evaluation. The reported correlations therefore establish fitted agreement, while predictive claims require independent evaluation or narrower wording. Moreover, Section 4.3 defines generalizable orientations by thresholding this fitted output, so their accuracy separation in Figure S.6 is not independent confirmation. Report fitting/evaluation separation and sensitivity to the 10% threshold.

Necessary—validate the interpretation of the invariance metric. Equations 5–7 compare activations averaged over orientation sets; equal averages can conceal strongly view-dependent responses. Requiring both averages to exceed the 95th-percentile threshold also excludes cases where a neuron responds strongly in one set but weakly in the other, making comparisons depend on which pairs survive selection. Report retained-pair counts and threshold sensitivity, and include an orientation-resolved check before interpreting these scores as evidence of neuronal invariance.

Necessary—complete the evaluation reporting. Specify test-image construction, orientation-grid resolution, samples per cell, and the meaning of plotted error bars. Clarify the observational unit in Figure 4: the prose describes instance- or orientation-level points, whereas Equation 7 aggregates across neurons and instances. Quantify correlations with uncertainty reflecting independent experimental repetitions. Also qualify the claim that increasing fully-seen diversity improves accuracy across conditions: several β and α′ conditions in Figure 3a show little clear increase.

Optional improvements: discuss how uniform Euler-angle sampling weights physical orientations nonuniformly, and enlarge the dense quantitative plots. Uniform-SO(3) sampling and more varied rendering conditions would improve external validity, but are not prerequisites if conclusions remain scoped to the studied setting.
